## Where we are

At this point you have:

. . .

✅ &nbsp; A reproducible project following the IPO protocol (`bigsss-repo/`)

. . .

✅ &nbsp; A local Git repository with a full commit history

. . .

✅ &nbsp; That repository live on GitHub at `github.com/phd-bigsss/bigsss-repo`

. . .

One step remains:

> Turning your Quarto HTML report into a **public website**  
> anyone can visit without installing R.

---

## What is GitHub Pages?

GitHub Pages is a **free static website hosting service** built into GitHub.

. . .

You point it at a folder or branch in your repo that contains HTML files.  
GitHub serves those files as a website at a public URL:

```
https://phd-bigsss.github.io/bigsss-repo
```

. . .

No server to configure. No hosting bill. No WordPress.  
The website updates every time you push new HTML to GitHub.

---

## Why it works perfectly with Quarto

When you run `quarto render` on your `.qmd` file, you get:

```
main_document.html    ← a complete, self-contained HTML file
```

. . .

GitHub Pages serves HTML files. Quarto produces HTML files.

. . .

```
quarto render → main_document.html → git push → GitHub Pages → public URL
```

. . .

The Quarto report you built in Part 1 is **already the right format**.  
We just need to tell GitHub where to find it.

---

## Two publishing approaches

There are two standard ways to connect Quarto to GitHub Pages.

. . .

**Approach A — `/docs` folder**

Render your document into a `/docs` subfolder, commit it, and tell GitHub Pages to serve from there.

```yaml
# _quarto.yml
output-dir: docs
```

You manage what gets committed manually.

. . .

**Approach B — `quarto publish`**

Run one command. Quarto renders the document, creates a dedicated `gh-pages` branch, and pushes the HTML automatically.

```bash
quarto publish gh-pages
```

GitHub Pages is configured to serve from that branch.

---

## Which approach today?

**We will use `quarto publish gh-pages`.**

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Why not `/docs`?**

- Requires committing rendered HTML into the `main` branch
- Mixing source files and output in the same commit history
- More manual steps to get right
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Why `quarto publish`?**

- One command does everything
- Rendered output lives in a separate branch — history stays clean
- Works the same way regardless of OS
- This is the approach Quarto's own documentation recommends
:::

::::

---

## What `quarto publish gh-pages` does

Under the hood, in one command:

. . .

1. Renders your `.qmd` to HTML with `self-contained: true`
2. Creates a `gh-pages` branch in your repo (if it does not exist)
3. Pushes the rendered HTML to that branch
4. GitHub Pages detects the branch and deploys the site

. . .

On your `main` branch, **nothing changes** — your source files stay clean.

. . .

```
main branch       processing/  input/  output/  main_document.qmd  README.md
gh-pages branch   index.html   (rendered output only)
```

---

## One required YAML change

Before publishing, add `self-contained: true` to your document's YAML header.

```yaml
---
title: "Study Report"
author: "Julio"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
    theme: cosmo
    code-fold: true
    self-contained: true    # ← add this line
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---
```

. . .

Without it, the HTML file references external CSS and JS files that GitHub Pages cannot find.  
With it, everything is bundled into a single portable `.html` file.

---

## The publish command

From the **RStudio Terminal** tab, inside your project folder:

```bash
quarto publish gh-pages
```

. . .

You will see:

```
? Publish update to: » https://phd-bigsss.github.io/bigsss-repo/ (GitHub Pages)
[Y/n]
```

Press `Y` and Enter.

. . .

Quarto renders, pushes, and prints your live URL.  
GitHub takes about **1–2 minutes** to deploy — then the site is live.

---

## The update cycle

After the first publish, updating your site is two steps:

. . .

**1. Edit your document**

Make any change to `main_document.qmd` — add a paragraph, update a table, fix a label.

. . .

**2. Publish again**

```bash
quarto publish gh-pages
```

. . .

That's it. The live website updates within a minute or two.

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
You still commit your source file changes to `main` as usual with Git.  
`quarto publish` handles the `gh-pages` branch separately — you never touch it directly.
:::

## Linking everything together

Update your `README.md` to include the Pages link:

```markdown
# bigsss-repo

Reproducible research project following the IPO protocol.

## Live report

📄 [View the report](https://phd-bigsss.github.io/bigsss-repo)

## Repository structure

input/       Raw and processed data
processing/  Analysis scripts
output/      Tables and figures
```

. . .

Now anyone who visits your GitHub repo sees the live link immediately.

---

## The full open science workflow

```
Research question
      ↓
IPO protocol           (Part 1 — project structure, R scripts, Quarto)
      ↓
Version control        (Part 2 — Git: every decision is traceable)
      ↓
GitHub                 (Part 2 — remote backup, shareable, citable)
      ↓
GitHub Pages           (Part 2 — report as a public website)
      ↓
OSF / Zenodo           (future — persistent DOI, preregistration)
```

. . .

> From raw data to a public, reproducible, citable research report —  
> using only tools you already have open on your screen.

---

## What the site looks like

Your GitHub repo and published site work as a pair:

. . .

| `github.com/phd-bigsss/bigsss-repo` | `phd-bigsss.github.io/bigsss-repo` |
|---|---|
| Source code, scripts, data | Rendered HTML report |
| Commit history and diffs | What a reader sees |
| For collaborators and reviewers | For everyone else |

. . .

Both URLs are worth sharing — the repo for transparency,  
the Pages site for accessibility.
